questions.question: What responsibility belongs to an Oozie coordinator rather than to a workflow?
options: Running one action graph from start to end
Creating workflow runs from nominal times and declared data availability
Executing every Hive query inside the Oozie server process
Replacing the Hadoop resource manager
questions.explanation: A workflow defines one acyclic action graph. A coordinator creates instances of that workflow according to schedule and data predicates.

questions.question: A dataset directory exists, but its producer is still uploading files. Which readiness contract most clearly prevents early consumption?
options: An empty done-flag that accepts directory existence
A producer-owned completion marker such as _SUCCESS
A shorter coordinator frequency
A larger Oozie server heap
questions.explanation: A completion marker separates partial publication from committed availability. Directory existence alone is unsafe when producers write incrementally.

questions.question: How do nominal time and actual time differ for a coordinator action?
options: Nominal time identifies the intended dataset slot; actual time records when processing really starts or occurs
Nominal time is always copied from the worker clock after completion
Actual time determines the coordinator's application XML namespace
They must be identical or submission fails
questions.explanation: Nominal time is the logical schedule position used to resolve dataset instances. Data delay and cluster pressure can make actual execution later.

questions.question: Why should every Oozie action have explicit success and error transitions?
options: They increase HDFS replication
They make the graph's next state and kill path deterministic
They encrypt credentials
They turn a workflow into a cyclic graph
questions.explanation: Oozie follows transitions after an action completes. Explicit error paths route failures to a reviewed recovery or kill node instead of leaving failure behavior ambiguous.

questions.question: A remote API committed a charge, but the action lost the acknowledgement and Oozie reports failure. What must happen before replay?
options: Blindly rerun the entire bundle
Reconcile the destination by a stable operation ID and ensure the write is idempotent
Delete the Oozie metadata database
Switch the coordinator execution strategy to LIFO
questions.explanation: Oozie can replay orchestration work but cannot infer whether a remote side effect committed. Reconciliation and idempotency contain the ambiguous outcome.

questions.question: What does the coordinator rerun option -refresh change?
options: It upgrades the Oozie server
It re-evaluates dataset dependencies such as latest() and future() for the rerun
It guarantees remote effects execute exactly once
It disables coordinator timeouts permanently
questions.explanation: A refreshed coordinator rerun rechecks data dependencies. It does not provide transaction guarantees for external systems.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes Oozie high availability?
options: Multiple Oozie servers remove every dependency failure
Multiple servers can protect the Oozie service, but the shared database, ZooKeeper ensemble, load balancer, Hadoop services, and log access remain dependencies
HA makes action output idempotent
HA removes the need for consistent server configuration
questions.explanation: Oozie HA covers the scheduler service. Full availability still depends on its shared state, coordination, routing, execution, storage, and observability systems.

questions.question: What is the most important platform fact when deciding whether to keep or migrate an Oozie estate in 2026?
options: Oozie is the newest active Apache orchestrator
Apache Oozie retired to the Apache Attic in 2025, so teams must own maintenance risk and compare migration cost with continued operation
Every Oozie workflow can be mechanically translated to Airflow
The Apache Attic provides new security releases
questions.explanation: Retirement means the Apache project no longer provides an active development community or future releases. Existing deployments may still run, but maintenance ownership and migration planning must be explicit.
